extracted.intended_audience: readers/students of Horace and classical Latin poetry; general readers interested in moral and poetic precepts
extracted.subtask_description: Reading and interpreting Horace's Satires and First Book of the Epistles, extracting their prescriptive moral and artistic maxims for personal conduct and poetic practice. Focuses on Horace's advice about virtue, self-mastery, study, and the aims of a poet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Renounce ludicrous verses; pursue truth and fitting subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet renounces all verses of a ludicrous turn, and resolves to apply himself wholly to the study of philosophy, which teaches to bridle the desires, and to postpone every thing to virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Horace states he will 'lay aside both verses, and all other sportive matters; my study and inquiry is after what is true and fitting,' indicating a deliberate move from light/jesting poetry toward serious, morally instructive subject matter and a disciplined poetic purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collect and preserve practical rules for later use
rubrics_metrics.description: I lay up, and collect rules which I may be able hereafter to bring into use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Horace recommends accumulating rules and principles (literary and ethical) to apply when needed, implying a craftsman's approach to poetic practice: learn, codify, and apply rules rather than relying solely on inspiration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be independent of any single master’s dogma
rubrics_metrics.description: Addicted to swear implicitly to the ipse-dixits of no particular master; wherever the weather drives me, I am carried a guest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Horace cautions against blind adherence to one school's dicta. He favors eclecticism and personal judgment over slavish imitation of a single philosophical or poetic authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temper desires; pursue virtue over external goods
rubrics_metrics.description: It is virtue, to fly vice; and the highest wisdom, to have lived free from folly... Silver is less valuable than gold, gold than virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated moral axiom: prioritize virtue above wealth, fame, or sensual pleasure. For a poet (and person), the proper aim is ethical excellence rather than accumulation of material rewards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin cultivation of wisdom and discipline early
rubrics_metrics.description: Boldly undertake the study of true wisdom: begin it forthwith... Now, while you are young, with an untainted mind Imbibe instruction: now apply yourself to the best [masters of morality].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Horace stresses the importance of early, sustained study and formation: learning good habits and moral instruction when young preserves them like a cask preserving flavor when new.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set a limit to desires; avoid covetousness
rubrics_metrics.description: To him that has got a competency, let him wish for no more... The covetous man is ever in want; set a certain limit to your wishes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical counsel to be content with enough; unchecked desire breeds perpetual dissatisfaction—relevant to artistic ambition and to the life conditions that support creative work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule your passions; restrain rage and excess
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule your passion, which commands, if it do not obey; do you restrain it with a bridle, and with fetters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes self-control: passions must be governed by reason. Horace uses the image of bridle and fetters—discipline (ethical and temperamental) is a criterion for the wise person and the reliable writer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inner character conditions the value of external goods (vessel metaphor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless the vessel be sweet, whatever you pour into it turns sour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Horace argues that external advantages (wealth, honors, art objects) are worthless if the person's inner moral 'vessel' is corrupt; applied to artists, technical skill or material success cannot redeem a corrupted character or purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid inconstancy and vacillation in judgment and life
rubrics_metrics.description: What do you do, when my judgment contradicts itself? it despises what it before desired; seeks for that which lately it neglected; is all in a ferment, and is inconsistent in the whole tenor of life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Horace criticizes fickleness—changing tastes, opinions, and lifestyles—and presents steadiness of purpose as an ideal. For writers, consistency of judgment and cultivated taste matters for credibility and craft.

rubrics_metrics.name: The wise man is self-mastering and therefore truly free
rubrics_metrics.description: Who then is free? The wise man, who has dominion over himself; whom neither poverty, nor death, nor chains affright; brave in the checking of his appetites, and in contemning honors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Horace defines freedom as internal mastery rather than external status. This criterion privileges moral/psychological autonomy as the highest good for life and by extension for the disposition required of a serious poet or moral teacher.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical living: use what you have and share convivial pleasures moderately
rubrics_metrics.description: If you can repose yourself as my guest... I will expect you... Dismiss airy hopes, and contests about riches... We shall have free liberty to prolong the summer evening with friendly conversation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice on modest, clean, cheerful hospitality and conviviality: favoring moderate, honest pleasures and fellowship over ostentatious display—an ethical stance that informs the social atmosphere appropriate to Horatian poetry.
